notes.meaning: Cornelius met Peter at the door and fell to the ground to show him deep honor. Because an angel had told him to send for Peter, Cornelius treated him with extraordinary reverence. Dropping to the ground before a mortal man went too far, even though Cornelius meant well.

Peter quickly pulled Cornelius to his feet and told him to stand up. He explained that he was only a human being just like Cornelius, so he should not be treated like a divine being. True worship belongs to God alone.

differ.view: John Calvin argued that Peter rejected this act because religious bowing belongs to God alone, showing that believers should not offer special spiritual honor to holy men or angels.

notes.meaning: Peter talked naturally with Cornelius as they stepped inside the house. There he found a large crowd of relatives and close friends waiting for him. They were eager to hear the message God had given Peter to deliver.

Peter reminded the group that Jewish customs forbade Jews from visiting or eating with Gentiles. However, God had recently taught Peter through a heavenly vision that no human being should be called impure or unclean. God was tearing down the old wall of separation between peoples.

Because God gave this instruction, Peter came right away without raising any objections. He then asked Cornelius why he had sent for him. This gave Cornelius the chance to share his story openly with everyone in the room.

Cornelius explained that four days earlier, he was praying at home around three in the afternoon. Suddenly, an angel resembling a man in radiant clothing stood right before him. The bright clothing showed that the visitor came directly from the presence of God.

The angel told Cornelius that God had heard his prayers and noticed his generous gifts to the poor. God accepted his sincere seeking as a sign of a tender heart. Still, these good deeds could not save him without faith in Christ.

The angel told Cornelius to send messengers to Joppa to invite Simon Peter to his home. Peter was staying by the sea at the house of a leather worker named Simon. God used an angel to set up the meeting, but he chose a human preacher to share the message of salvation.

Cornelius explained that he sent for Peter right away, and he thanked Peter for being willing to come. The whole household had gathered in the presence of God to listen with open hearts. They were eager to hear every single command the Lord had given Peter to speak.

Peter began his sermon by stating that he now clearly understood that God does not play favorites. God does not accept people simply because they are Jewish, nor does he reject others just because they are Gentiles. True acceptance before God does not depend on a person's race or national heritage.

In every nation, God welcomes anyone who fears him and does what is right. Peter did not mean that good deeds earn salvation, but that a reverent heart and upright living show God's grace is at work. God welcomes all who seek him, no matter where they come from.

differ.view: John Piper emphasizes that Cornelius was not yet saved before hearing Peter preach, but that God was pleased with his genuine search and brought him the gospel so he could be saved through faith.
Charles Ellicott notes that Cornelius already had true faith and was accepted by God through grace, even though he did not yet know about Jesus by name.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some Catholic writers cite the case of Cornelius to show that God can give grace and salvation to non-Christians who seek him sincerely, outside the normal sacrament of baptism.

notes.meaning: God first delivered this message to the people of Israel, announcing peace between God and humanity through Jesus Christ. Peter added that Jesus is Lord over all people, Jews and Gentiles alike. Because Jesus rules over everyone, the offer of salvation belongs to all nations.

Peter reminded his listeners of events they had already heard about throughout the region of Judea. The story of Jesus began in Galilee right after John the Baptist preached his baptism of repentance. These well-known historical events formed the groundwork for the good news.

God anointed Jesus with the Holy Spirit and with power at his baptism, setting him apart for his sacred work. Jesus spent his ministry traveling around doing good and healing everyone under the devil's cruel power. He was able to do this because God was with him in all his work.

Peter declared that the apostles were eyewitnesses of everything Jesus did across the countryside and in Jerusalem. Even though Jesus did only good, the authorities put him to death by hanging him on a wooden cross. The apostles were called to bear honest witness to these historical facts.

On the third day after his death, God raised Jesus back to life by divine power. God did not leave him in the grave, but caused him to appear openly and visibly. This proved beyond doubt that his sacrifice was accepted by God.

Jesus did not appear to the general public after his resurrection, but to witnesses God had specially chosen in advance. The apostles were certain he was truly alive because they spent time with him and ate and drank in his presence. This showed he had a real physical body and was not a ghost or hallucination.

Jesus commanded the apostles to preach to the people and bear witness about his authority. God appointed Jesus to be the Judge of the living and the dead, which means every person who has ever lived must answer to him. Our eternal future depends on turning to him as Lord and Savior.

All the Old Testament prophets pointed to Jesus and agreed on his mission. They foretold that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through the power of his name. This pardon is offered freely to anyone who puts their trust in him.

While Peter was still speaking, the Holy Spirit suddenly came down upon all the Gentiles who were listening to the message. God did not wait for Peter to finish his sermon or for water baptism to take place. By pouring out his Spirit, God proved that he had fully accepted these Gentile believers.

The Jewish believers who had traveled with Peter from Joppa were completely astonished. They had assumed the Holy Spirit was promised only to the Jewish people. Seeing the Spirit poured out on uncircumcised Gentiles opened their eyes to God's wider plan of mercy.

The Jewish believers knew the Holy Spirit had come because they heard the Gentiles speaking in unfamiliar languages and praising God. The Gentiles used these miraculous tongues to give glory to God for his wonderful salvation. This miracle matched what had happened to Jewish believers on the day of Pentecost.

differ.view: Pentecostals teach that speaking in tongues is the initial physical evidence of the baptism in the Holy Spirit, which is an experience distinct from and following conversion.

Many evangelicals believe speaking in tongues here was a unique sign given to convince Jewish believers that Gentiles were equal members in the church, rather than a pattern required for all Christians.

notes.meaning: Peter asked whether anyone could object to baptizing these Gentiles in water, since they had already received the Holy Spirit just like the Jewish believers. If God had given them the inner reality of the Spirit, no one could deny them the outward water. Baptism was the proper sign to welcome them into the fellowship of the church.

differ.view: John Calvin argued that because the Spirit was given before baptism, spiritual grace is not locked inside the water, yet baptism remains the necessary outward sign of faith for those God adopts.
Adam Clarke noted that although these believers had already become part of Christ's spiritual body, water baptism was still required to enter the visible Christian church.

Many Baptists and evangelicals point to this verse as evidence that baptism does not save or wash away sins, because Cornelius received the Holy Spirit and forgiveness before water baptism took place.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching notes that while God normally works through the sacraments, he is not bound by them, so he gave the Holy Spirit before water baptism in this unique instance.

notes.meaning: Peter ordered that the new believers be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, likely having his Jewish companions perform the baptisms. After being baptized, the new converts begged Peter to stay with them for a few days. They were hungry to be taught more about their new life in Christ.
